name: Huriez syndrome
aliases: scleroatrophic and keratotic dermatosis of the limbs

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis combining a diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma with scleroatrophy of the hands and feet and nail abnormalities
Caused by variants affecting SMARCAD1, in particular disruption of a skin-specific promoter of this chromatin-remodelling gene
The distal limbs show sclerodactyly with atrophic, shiny skin and hypoplastic or absent nails
The hallmark and most serious feature is a markedly increased risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising within the keratotic, scleroatrophic skin, typically in early to middle adult life
Hypohidrosis and a fixed, tight appearance of the acral skin are characteristic
Diagnosis is clinical with family history, supported by biopsy and molecular testing; any non-healing or changing lesion warrants biopsy
Management combines supportive keratolytic and emollient skin care with lifelong surveillance for cutaneous malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Huriez syndrome is associated with variants affecting SMARCAD1, a chromatin-remodelling enzyme, particularly a mutation in a skin-specific promoter that reduces its expression in the epidermis. Impaired chromatin remodelling disturbs keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation and genomic stability, producing the diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and the scleroatrophic changes of the distal limbs with nail hypoplasia. The same disturbance predisposes the affected skin to malignant transformation, accounting for the characteristically early and aggressive squamous cell carcinomas that dominate the prognosis.
additionalDifferentials: Acrogeria and other acral atrophic syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of suspicious or non-healing lesions to detect squamous cell carcinoma
Regular full skin and acral examination for malignant change
Imaging and lymph node assessment if invasive carcinoma is confirmed
redFlags: Any non-healing ulcer, nodule or changing lesion within scleroatrophic skin, given the high squamous carcinoma risk
Regional lymphadenopathy suggesting metastatic squamous cell carcinoma
Recurrent secondary infection of atrophic acral skin
reference.prognosis: Skin and nail changes are chronic but stable; prognosis is dominated by the lifelong risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma, which can metastasise and be fatal, making early detection through surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Mistaking the sclerodactyly for systemic sclerosis and missing the genodermatosis and its cancer risk
Failing to biopsy non-healing lesions in scleroatrophic skin
Underestimating the aggressiveness of squamous cell carcinoma in this setting
management: Lifelong skin surveillance with regular full-skin and acral examination and a low threshold to biopsy any non-healing or changing lesion for squamous cell carcinoma
Prompt wide surgical excision of squamous cell carcinoma with lymph node assessment and imaging for metastatic spread
Topical emollients and keratolytics such as urea and salicylic acid, with oral retinoids for severe palmoplantar keratoderma
Sun protection and avoidance of cutaneous carcinogens to limit further malignant risk
Hand and foot functional support and wound care for the scleroatrophic skin and nail changes
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant SMARCAD1 inheritance and family screening
Multidisciplinary care with dermatology, surgical oncology and clinical genetics
